title: Update Software
summary: Updating software is the systematic replacement of vulnerable code with vendor-fixed versions across every asset class an organisation operates, from operating systems and hypervisors through network appliances, container base images, firmware, and third-party libraries. The operational reality is dominated by inventory and scheduling rather than by the patch action itself, because you cannot update what you do not know exists. The control therefore rests on authoritative asset discovery, software composition analysis, a bill of materials for everything the organisation builds, and a change process capable of reaching production servers, field devices, remote laptops, and appliances that are only manageable through a vendor console. Effective programmes rank risk instead of chasing one score: vendor severity, evidence of exploitation in the wild, and whether the asset is internet-facing jointly decide what enters an emergency channel with a short deadline, while lower-risk internal findings wait for a scheduled ring. Where patching is genuinely impossible, teams apply compensating controls and record time-boxed risk acceptance with a named owner. The control breaks the most common initial-access path, exploitation of unpatched public-facing applications and remote-access gateways, and it removes the client-side and local privilege-escalation flaws that follow user execution. Its limitations are well understood: firmware and industrial systems rarely tolerate a reboot, shadow IT and embedded appliances escape inventory, vendors ship delayed or partial fixes, zero-days exist before patches do, and the update channel is itself a supply-chain target. Updating also fails quietly when installation reports success but the service is never restarted, or when an old container image is rescheduled from a registry that still holds it.
objectives: Explain how asset inventory, composition analysis, and risk ranking combine to produce a defensible patch cadence.
Distinguish emergency remediation of internet-facing systems from routine monthly rings and define the trigger for each.
Identify the asset classes that routinely escape inventory and describe how to bring them under management.
Apply compensating controls and time-boxed risk acceptance where patching genuinely cannot occur.
Assess the supply-chain risk introduced by the software update channel itself.
Verify that a patch has taken effect at runtime rather than trusting successful installation output.
Prioritise remediation using vendor severity, exploitation evidence, and exposure together.
